title: The Height of a Bowed Head
logline: A manor house begun about 1700 was added to by six generations until it held a hundred and twenty-one rooms and twenty-one courtyards, and every doorway in it was cut to about five feet, so that nobody could come in with their head up; forty-three rooms are left, and the doorways are still that height.
human_question: If what somebody wanted was not goods but the sight of other people lowering their heads, and they built it into a doorway you can measure in feet and inches, is the wanting now visible — or only the doorway?

place.what_kind_of_place: A single-storey manor house of clay-and-brick walls and hand-cut timber, standing on a low stone platform at the edge of a small inland town in hill country, and now a state museum under the national archaeology department. It was not designed and built once. It was begun about 1700 as one building and then added to across six generations, rooms attached to rooms and courtyards opened inside courtyards, the last of the adding finished in 1905, until it held a hundred and twenty-one rooms and twenty-one open inner courtyards inside a single roofed plan. Forty-three rooms and seven courtyards are what is left. There is no second storey worth the name and no grand hall; the plan is a maze of small rooms strung on corridors, with the courtyards punched through it as the only source of daylight and the only way rain leaves the building, through channels cut in the floors. Every doorway in the house is about five feet high. Outside the main plan, in the grounds, stand the outbuildings of a private jurisdiction: a court room with bench seating for about a hundred people, its furniture still standing where it stood, a line of faded British-era lettering on the back wall, and a small holding cell off the side of it.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: It is a film made entirely of doorways and light, and both are already in the building. Because the courtyards are the only openings, the interior is almost black except where a hard-edged shaft of daylight drops through a courtyard doorway and lies on a floor, and that rectangle moves across the room all day without anybody touching it. The doorways line up: stand in the right place and there are five or six low openings inside one another, each one a smaller rectangle of light in the dark, and the far end of the house is a bright postage stamp at the end of them. And the rooms are empty. Lime-plastered walls, a floor, a beam, dust turning in the shaft, and nothing else — so the low rectangle of the doorway is the only thing in the frame with a measurement, which is exactly what the film is about. There is one other surface worth a lens of its own: a mosaic floor laid in 1905 out of deliberately broken imported plate, set face up, with the fragments of royal portraits and currency marks in it, photographed at macro from a foot above the ground.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing, and none of it is the crew's. The sun crosses each courtyard and drags a bright rectangle across a floor, up a wall and out; a room that was unwatchable at ten is the best shot in the house at one. When it rains the whole interior goes blue-grey and flat, the courtyards run, the cut channels do the job they were made for, and the sound of the building changes completely. Bats live in the upper structure and the air says so. Dust hangs in every shaft of light and settles when the light goes. The only other movement is the camera's own, and its one recurring move is to lower itself to get under a lintel.
place.when_it_looks_best: Mid-morning to early afternoon, when the sun is high enough to fall into small courtyards and actually reach the floors of the rooms off them; the doorway-inside-doorway shots want the hour either side of noon, when the far courtyard is brightest and the corridor between is darkest. A wet afternoon in either monsoon gives the film its second look, with no shafts at all and the whole interior one soft grey. Late afternoon is for the closing frame, when the rectangle slides off the floor and the far room stops being visible through the door.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A slow, quiet, entirely interior film about an old house that has lost two-thirds of itself. No aerial shot, no crowd, no golden hour on a monument, no music cue at a reveal — a camera held low, moving through a run of five-foot doorways one at a time, dipping under each lintel, into rooms with nothing in them where a single shaft of daylight is doing all the work. It has its own shape: in at a gate, through the plan, out into the grounds where the court room is, back in for the rain, and then a last doorway held until the light goes out of it. A viewer who never hears a word of the narration gets the strangest domestic interior in the country, the arithmetic of a hundred and twenty-one down to forty-three, and a very simple piece of suspense: how low is that door, and who was it low for?
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the group's hardest case, because the wanting here was not for goods. The books this series reads keep a list of the ordinary occasions on which greed-rooted minds come up, and preparing and using the things one likes — clothes, houses, carriages — is on it, along with a line about wanting to appear as a superior person. This building is that list turned into masonry across two centuries, and the thing it was built to obtain was deference, at a height anybody can measure. Then the same books supply the counterweight the film cannot do without: the wish to do a thing is not greed, it has no side of its own, and effort is defined as mental rather than bodily and is refused the status of a virtue. Which leaves the film where the group needs it. The doorway is five feet. Everything the books are actually talking about — the feeling, the view, whether the mind was prompted — is not in the frame at all, and the voice says so rather than pretending the camera has caught somebody out.

sequence.on_screen: Ground level, outside, square on: a low stone gateway in a boundary wall, with a drive and a dark verandah beyond it. The camera moves through the opening and the underside of the arch passes just above the lens. Nothing else of the exterior is shown.
sequence.voice: The books this series reads keep a list of the ordinary occasions when a greed-rooted mind comes up. Good food, sweet drinks, music, fine clothes. Earning money, getting it, guarding it, spending it on something you like. And then, in the same breath: preparing the things you like — clothes, houses, carriages — and using them. A house is on the list. This one was on it for two hundred years.

sequence.on_screen: Inside. Five or six doorways in line down the long axis of the plan, each a low rectangle inside the last, the far one bright. The camera holds, then goes through them one at a time, lowering itself under every lintel. The dip of the lens is the only measurement the film offers.
sequence.voice: Every door in this house is about five feet high. Why is not agreed. One account says the gateways were cut low so that a visitor arriving on horseback had to get down. One says anyone entering had to bow. And one says the man who finished the house was four feet eight inches tall, so that he alone could ride straight in with his head up while everybody else bent. Those are three different reasons and they do not all fit together. The height is the same whichever one you take.

sequence.on_screen: The accretion. A courtyard open to the sky, plastered walls, a channel cut across the floor for rain; through a low doorway on the far side, a second courtyard behind it. Then a corridor with closed doors down both sides. Then three empty rooms in a row, each darker than the last.
sequence.voice: It began about 1700 as one building, and six generations went on adding to it. At its largest it held a hundred and twenty-one rooms and twenty-one courtyards, and the last of the adding was done in 1905. The list in the books is not a list of crimes. It is a list of occasions. This is a building made of nothing else — occasions, in brick, one after another, for two centuries.

sequence.on_screen: One room with nothing in it. A hard shaft of daylight from the courtyard doorway lies across the floor; dust turns in it. Then close: a hand-cut joint in the roof timber, the grain of a jamb worn smooth at shoulder height, and the 1905 floor at macro — smashed imported plate laid face up, a fragment of a royal portrait, a currency mark.
sequence.voice: Here the same books stop and make a distinction. The wish to do a thing, they say, is not greed. Greed is the sticking. The wish is only the wanting to take something up, and it has no side of its own: put it in a grasping mind and it strengthens the grasping, put it in a good one and it works against it. They say the same of effort, and they are careful — effort in these books is mental, not the strength in anybody's arms. Every joint in this roof was cut by somebody with that wish and that effort in them. So was every school and every well in the country. The wood does not say which.

sequence.on_screen: One held frame in an outbuilding, no camera movement at all. A long room with bench seating for about a hundred, the furniture standing where it stands, a line of faded lettering along the back wall, and the closed door of a small side room. The camera stays at the back of the room. Nothing in it is approached, lit or picked out.
sequence.voice: One room on this ground is not a room of the house. A hundred people could sit in it while one man judged land, cattle and marriages. The furniture is still in it. So, the record says, is the equipment that was used for punishment. That is on the record, and this film leaves it there. What these books count is never a room and never a building. They separate one of these minds from another by three things — whether the feeling in it was pleasant or level, whether a wrong view was joined to it, and whether it came up on its own or was prompted. Not one of those three can be photographed.

sequence.on_screen: Rain. The courtyards running, water finding the cut channels in the floors, the whole interior gone flat blue-grey with no shaft in it anywhere. Roof timbers from below. Then the plan read straight down a corridor, door after door after door, to a grey rectangle at the end.
sequence.voice: The books put effort in a picture. It is a boat on a current: in a mind already tilted, it carries the mind along without being asked, and doing good, they say, is like carrying a load up a hill. So effort is not a virtue in them. Nor is gladness — they describe that as the mind swelling open like a flower, and they let it turn up in a bad mind as readily as a good one. Trained, they say, the wish to do becomes a base of success and can carry somebody the whole way to what they are after. It also added rooms here for two hundred years.

sequence.on_screen: Late light. One empty room as the bright rectangle slides off the floor, up the wall and out. Then back to a single doorway, the camera set at the height of a bowed head, held without moving until the room on the other side of it is too dark to see.
sequence.voice: A hundred and twenty-one rooms; forty-three left. That is not a verdict on anybody, and these books do not offer one — they classify a mind for as long as it lasts, not a person and not a family. What can be measured here is a doorway. Five feet, near enough, in a wall that is still standing, and it will make the next person who walks through it lower their head. Whether anything was wanted, and what, was never in the building.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, C005 is not a list of sins; it is a list of occasions, and one of its entries is the whole subject of this film. The Margaya's long enumeration runs from liquor, gambling and bribes through music, perfume, fine clothes and tasty food to doing many things in order to acquire wealth, acquiring it, guarding what has been acquired, spending it to obtain the objects one likes, and then preparing the objects one likes — clothes, houses, carriages — and consuming them [C005-M:L5]. A house that was added to for two hundred years is that line, in brick. The same source then names the aim that this particular house makes measurable: preparing and wearing clothes out of a wish to be beautiful, to win others over, or to appear as a superior person is greed-rooted [C005-M:L15], while a good or even valuable garment worn to escape the contempt of onlookers is not counted unwholesome [C005-M:L19], and acts done with faith, loving-kindness, compassion or a practical sense of what is useful are not counted unwholesome either [C005-M:L9]. So the source's own line is drawn between escaping contempt and obtaining superiority, which is precisely the line a doorway cut to five feet stands on and cannot be made to declare. And the source is explicit that what is being sorted is a mind and not a person or a thing: the eight greed-rooted minds are separated from one another by feeling, by whether a wrong view is joined, and by whether the mind was prompted or arose unprompted [C005-P:L12] [C005-P:L27–L42]. None of those three is a photographable property of a building. C021 supplies the honest counterweight without which this film would be an accusation. The six occasional factors run through wholesome and unwholesome minds alike and are reckoned by the mind they join [C021-P:L25]; desire-to-act is the wish to take up an object [C021-P:L69] or the wish to do [C021-M:L27], lacking greed's stickiness, supporting greed inside a greed-rooted mind and opposing it inside a wholesome one [C021-P:L75]; effort is mental rather than bodily and is the not-turning-back that goes on until a started thing is finished [C021-M:L19], pictured as a boat on a downstream current that carries a tilted mind along while doing good is like carrying a load uphill [C021-P:L53]; and gladness is the mind swelling open like a flower [C021-M:L23]. A building accreted over six generations is made of exactly those factors and shows none of their colour.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the group's subject is not appetite for goods and never was. It is stickiness, and the thing stuck to here is other people's posture. C005 on its own reads, to an ordinary listener, as a verdict on ordinary pleasures, which its own digest denies; C021 on its own is a parts list. Put on this building they produce the one film in the group where the wanted thing is not a thing at all, was obtained architecturally, and survives as a number in feet and inches that anybody can check — while the mental event the books are actually classifying is as invisible in a five-foot doorway as it is in a market. That is the film's discipline and also its ending. It measures the doorway, it keeps the three incompatible explanations apart, it declines to say what was wanted, and when the house turns the other way — a hundred and twenty-one rooms down to forty-three — it refuses to read that as a judgement on anyone, because the sources classify a mind for as long as it lasts and not a person, a family or a line.

concept_links.why: The concept is the occasions on which greed-rooted minds arise, and this location is an occasion built out of masonry. The Margaya's list explicitly includes acquiring wealth, guarding what is acquired, spending it to obtain liked objects, and preparing and consuming liked objects including houses [C005-M:L5]; it also covers providing for spouses and children and says that for ordinary people most minds from waking until sleep are of this kind [C005-M:L7]. The film's own hinge is the source's aim-line about appearance: wanting to look beautiful, to win others over, or to appear as a superior person is greed-rooted [C005-M:L15], whereas wearing something good to escape onlookers' contempt is not counted unwholesome [C005-M:L19], and neither are acts led by faith, loving-kindness, compassion or practical discernment of usefulness [C005-M:L9]. A doorway that obliges everyone but its owner to lower their head sits exactly on that line and cannot be read off it, which is why the film states the competing explanations and stops. Four limits out of the digest are load-bearing and are written into the beats rather than left to a caution. The source classifies minds, not persons: the eight are told apart by feeling, by whether wrong view is joined, and by whether the mind was prompted or unprompted [C005-P:L12] [C005-P:L27–L42], so beat 5 says outright that none of the three can be photographed, and no visitor, guide or official in this film is framed as acquisitive. 'Only intentions matter' is not the source's position either, since it still names theft, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, idle chatter, covetousness and wrong view as courses of harm carried out through greed-rooted minds [C005-M:L3]; that is the honest reason the recorded existence of a private court and its punishment equipment is not suppressed, and the reason it is stated once and not toured. The digest's own uncertainty is respected: several of these cases are called only 'not unwholesome' without being told what they are instead [C005-M:L9] [C005-M:L19], so the film never upgrades anybody here to wholesome and never downgrades anybody either. And the remark that most of an ordinary day runs on greed-rooted minds [C005-M:L7] is the author's unquantified general statement; it is used as a description of how much of life runs on liking, never as a measurement and never aimed at the people who lived here.

This is the link that stops the film becoming a prosecution of a building. Both sources define desire-to-act as the wish to take up an object [C021-P:L69] or the wish to do [C021-M:L27], insist that it lacks the stickiness that belongs to greed, craving and longing, and say it follows the moral side of the mind it joins — accordant with greed in a greed-accompanied mind, opposed to greed in a mind opposed to greed [C021-M:L27]; the Pradeepika adds that it supports greed inside a greed-rooted mind, helps subdue greed inside a wholesome one, and developed becomes a predominant factor and a base of success leading to higher wholesome action, absorption and the end of craving [C021-P:L75]. The six factors are also stated to be scattered across wholesome and unwholesome minds alike and to be reckoned wholesome, unwholesome or indeterminate by the mind they join [C021-P:L25]. That is the sentence the whole film turns on, because the accretion of a house over six generations and the building of anything else whatever are the same factors at work. Effort is used exactly as the Margaya defines it — not turning back, going forward until the started thing is done, and mental rather than bodily, with bodily strength explicitly excluded from being a mental factor [C021-M:L19] — which is the cleanest statement in either digest of why a camera pointed at two hundred years of carpentry has photographed nothing of what matters. The digest's guards are what let this concept appear at all. 'Hard work is always virtuous' is ruled out by the boat on the downstream current, which carries a tilted mind along while doing good is like carrying a load up a hill [C021-P:L53], and beat 6 is built on that refusal rather than on admiration. 'Follow your passion' is ruled out because the same wish inside a greed-rooted mind strengthens the greed [C021-P:L75]. Gladness is taken only as far as the Margaya takes it, the mind swelling open like a flower [C021-M:L23]; the Pradeepika's air-element account of rapture shaking the body [C021-P:L61] is traditional physiology and is not used. And the digest's note that the deciding factor settles firmly on an object without separating true from false and is frequently wrong [C021-P:L45] is the reason the film treats none of the three explanations for the door heights as settled, including the one that is most satisfying to believe.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That wanting is not only wanting things — that it can be a wanting for other people's deference, and that somebody once built that into a doorway at a height you can put a tape on. That the books being quoted separate the wish to do something from the sticking that makes it grasping, so the same energy that accreted this house accretes everything anybody has ever finished. And that the difference between those two is the one thing in the building the camera cannot get at, which is why the film measures the door and stops there.
what_must_be_real: The door and ceiling heights are measured on site by the crew and stated as measured, not repeated from the web; if they come out differently from the published figures the film says the measured number. The three explanations for the low doorways are kept apart on screen and none is chosen, because they contradict each other. Nothing is dressed, moved, placed, swept or arranged in any room: the empty rooms are empty as found and the furniture is where the museum has it. No instrument of punishment appears in frame — the court room is filmed once, from the back, in a single held wide, and nothing in it is approached, lit, isolated or shot close; if that cannot be guaranteed the beat is cut. No descendant, community, caste or family is characterised, named or sought, and nobody living is implicated in anything recorded here; the aristocratic and colonial arrangement this house belonged to is described as a recorded arrangement, neither judged nor admired. The last master is named once, only because the door heights are documented against his own stated height; his life is not narrated and he is not a character. Anybody who appears in frame — a guide, a museum officer, a visitor — is there by informed consent, is never framed as acquisitive, deferential, curious or anything else a camera cannot see, and is not filmed at all if consent is doubtful. Light is whatever the building and the department allow; if artificial light is refused, the film is shot at the exposure the courtyards give and the dark stays dark.
position_hint: late in the group. It only does its work after the open-air films have shown wanting at its widest and most obvious, because its job is to move the group's subject off goods entirely and then refuse the conclusion that the camera has caught anybody at anything. It is also the group's only interior film and its slowest, so it should not be cut next to another quiet one. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: This group's specific problem, in its sharpest form: a camera cannot show greed. The sources sort minds by feeling, by whether wrong view is joined and by whether the mind was prompted [C005-P:L12] [C005-P:L27–L42], and a building declares none of it. No visitor, guide or official may be framed as acquisitive, and the film must not let a low doorway stand in as evidence of a state of mind.

Becoming a film about a family. There is no lineage story here, no rise, no fall, no decline and no 'what they left behind'; C061 states plainly that legacy and remembrance are not the teaching. The subject is a building and what was built into it, and the six generations are a fact about the masonry, not a saga.

The private court and its punishment equipment turning the film into a tour of cruelty. It is recorded once, factually, in a single held wide from the back of the room, with no instrument in frame and nothing dwelt on; if that discipline cannot be held on location the beat is dropped.

Adjudicating the colonial period, or narrating the arrangement as anyone's grievance or anyone's due. The anti-colonial reading of the low doorways is one of the accounts on the record and is presented as such, not as the meaning of the building.

Choosing between the three explanations for the door heights because one of them is the best story. They are incompatible; the digest's own note that the deciding factor settles firmly whether or not it is right [C021-P:L45] is a standing warning here.

Sanctifying or condemning anybody through C021. Effort and the wish to do are morally colourless in the sources, the boat runs downhill as easily as up [C021-P:L53], and two centuries of carpentry prove nothing about anyone.
Reading 'only intentions matter' into C005, which still names particular actions as courses of harm carried out through greed-rooted minds [C005-M:L3].

Preaching self-denial by implication. The source allows wealth earned and spent with discernment and even a valuable garment worn to escape contempt [C005-M:L9] [C005-M:L19]; a film about a large house must not slide into a lesson about owning less.

Filming permission. This is a department-of-archaeology museum, permission is a written application with stated sites, dates and reason and a script for a film, and at least one recent visitor account reports that photography and videography are prohibited on site outright. Permission may be refused or made conditional, and the whole film depends on it.
Light. The building has no windows to speak of and the courtyards are the only source; without permission for any supplementary light the interiors may be unusable at the contrast the film wants.

Health and conservation. Bats are living in the structure and the smell is reported as strong on the upper levels; damp and deteriorating plaster mean a crew must not touch, lean on or rig to anything.

Drone. It is not the tool for a forty-three-room single-storey interior and no aerial reveal belongs in this film; any use at all would need separate clearance and would be a liability rather than a gain.
drop_if: Filming permission for the interior is refused, or is granted only on terms that require showing what the film has decided not to show.
The court room cannot be filmed in one held wide without an instrument of punishment in frame, or cannot be filmed without a commentary that dwells on it.
The doorways cannot be measured on site, so the film would be repeating a published figure it has not checked.
Access is only possible as part of a guided visit whose narration must be recorded and used, which would hand the film a story about a family.
The interior cannot be shot at all without lighting the department will not permit, and the courtyard light alone does not carry the film.

connections.note: The film previously held in this record — a full-moon night when a junction town gave food away free — was dropped as a duplicate of IDEA-0059, which is already a Poson dansala road with hundreds of stalls giving food away. One such film in the series is enough, and IDEA-0059 is the one that keeps it. This record was rebuilt on an entirely different location and kind of place.
A room where nothing physically changes hands and the wanting is all in the bidding, and a house where nothing was bought and the wanting was for the way people came through a door.
Two films about the wish to do a thing rather than to have it, one in a workshop where the same energy is making something and one in a building where it went on adding rooms for two centuries.

selection.reason: Rebuilt from the ground up. The film it replaced duplicated IDEA-0059, and this group had fourteen candidates that were all working places, markets or trades with no historical story between them. This is now the group's only building, its only historical thread and its only interior film, and it carries the one case where what was wanted was not a thing.

review.note: Replaced entirely, and the previous verdict on this record refers to a film that no longer exists. Two reasons, both hard. First, the old film — a full-moon almsgiving night in an inland junction town, where the town's whole apparatus of appetite was turned around and food was given away free — duplicated IDEA-0059, which is already a film about exactly that: a Poson dansala road lined for kilometres with hundreds of stalls giving food away. Two dansala films in one series is a repeat, and this was the one that had to go. Second, this group was a monoculture: all fourteen candidates were working places, markets or trades, and not one of them rested on a historical story, which fails Chathura's decisions 4 and 5 at group level. The new film is bound to a documented history rather than to an analogy. An eighteenth-century manor house, begun on the site about 1700 in the reign of Vimaladharmasuriya II and added to by six generations, reached a hundred and twenty-one rooms and twenty-one inner courtyards, with its present layout owed largely to its last prominent figure, born in September 1844 and knighted; forty-three rooms remain. Every doorway is about five feet high, and the accounts of why disagree: that visitors arriving on horseback had to dismount, that anyone entering had to bow, and that the last master was four feet eight inches tall so that he alone could ride through with his head up. Those three are not compatible, they are held apart in what_is_disputed, and the film does not choose between them on screen. That is the binding: C005 is about the occasions on which greed-rooted minds arise, and this is a building that is nothing but occasions accreted in brick, with a wanting that was not for goods but for deference, built into the architecture at a measurable height — and then the house went the other way, a hundred and twenty-one rooms down to forty-three. C021 supplies the honest counterweight: desire-to-act is not greed, effort is mental and is not a virtue, and the distinction between the two is exactly what a camera cannot see, which the film says out loud in beat 5. Three constraints were treated as absolute. It is not a film about a family — no lineage, no rise and fall, no legacy, because C061 rules that out and the bar is live; the last master is named once, only because the door heights are documented against his own height. The private court and its punishment equipment are recorded in one held wide from the back of the room, factually, with no instrument in frame and nothing approached or isolated, and the beat is cut rather than softened if that cannot be guaranteed on site. And nobody living is implicated: no descendant, community or caste is characterised, and the aristocratic and colonial order the house belonged to is described as a recorded arrangement, neither judged nor admired. Treatment is the group's interior film and shares its approach with nothing else in the group — doorways, thresholds, courtyards, corridors, low ceilings, shafts of daylight in rooms with nothing in them, a camera held at the height of a bowed head, slow and enclosed and quiet where the rest of the group is open-air, crowded and fast, with no aerial reveal, because a house of forty-three rooms does not read from the sky. New title, with the old one kept in aliases. Both concept links were re-tested against their digests and rewritten from scratch: C005 re-grounded on the occasions list that includes preparing and using houses, on the aim-line that separates wanting to appear superior from wanting to escape contempt, and on the three conditions by which the eight greed-rooted minds are told apart, none of which is photographable; C021 re-grounded on desire-to-act as the wish to do, on effort as mental and not bodily, and on the boat-on-a-current refusal to treat effort as a virtue. Filming permission is a real requirement at a department-of-archaeology museum and one recent visitor account reports photography and videography prohibited outright, so that is recorded in access, risks, drop_if and unknowns rather than assumed away. Note for the record that this puts a second film in the same district as IDEA-0020 within this group; the location was assigned and the district concentration is flagged rather than resolved.

suggested_location.name: Maduwanwela Walauwa (Maduwanwela Walawwa)

also_known_as.name: meda midula
also_known_as.meaning: the open inner courtyard around which rooms are arranged; the house is counted in these as well as in rooms, and they are the only source of daylight inside the plan

also_known_as.name: walauwa
also_known_as.meaning: the manor house of a landed family holding office; the building type, used here for the kind of place rather than for any family

also_known_as.name: nindagama
also_known_as.meaning: a service-tenure estate held with an office; the term used in the sources for the land holding this house sat at the centre of

suggested_location.region: Ratnapura District, Sabaragamuwa Province: the low inland hill country at Kolonna, on the Embilipitiya–Rakwana road between the southern dry plains and the Rakwana massif, roughly 30 km from Embilipitiya and about 207 km from Colombo
suggested_location.why_here: Because the concept and the picture are the same object. C005 is about the occasions on which greed-rooted minds arise, and the Margaya's own list names preparing and consuming the objects one likes, houses among them. This is a house that was not designed but accumulated: begun as one building about 1700 and added to by six generations until it held 121 rooms and 21 inner courtyards inside one plan, with the last expansion in 1905. Then the concept's hardest version is here as a measurement. Every doorway in the building is about five feet high, and the recorded explanations for that disagree — so that riders had to dismount, so that everyone entering had to bow, and because the last master stood four feet eight inches, so that he alone could ride through with his head up. What was being obtained was not goods; it was posture, and it was specified in feet and inches and built. No other candidate in the group offers a wanting that is architectural rather than transactional. Cinematically it is the one place in the group that is entirely interior. Because the courtyards are the only openings, the whole building is dark except where a hard shaft of daylight lands, and the doorways line up so that five or six low openings nest inside one another with a bright rectangle at the end — which is the film's best frame and its clearest statement of its subject in the same shot. And the house then argues the other way by itself: 121 rooms down to 43, so the film ends on subtraction without needing a moral. The site is a state museum under the Department of Archaeology, which makes access formal, documented and refusable, and that is stated rather than wished away.
what_to_film: The run of doorways along the long axis, filmed as nested rectangles from a fixed low position, then again as a single continuous move through them with the camera lowering under each lintel. This is the film's spine.
One doorway measured on site, with the measurement visible in the frame, and the same doorway with the camera locked at the height of a bowed head.
A courtyard from inside the room next to it: the open square of sky, the plastered walls, the channel cut in the floor, and a second courtyard visible through the doorway beyond.
Three or four empty rooms at different hours, to get the shaft of daylight arriving, crossing the floor, climbing the wall and leaving.
Corridors, with closed doors down both sides, read straight down their length to a lit rectangle at the end.
The 1905 mosaic floor at macro from a foot above the ground: broken imported plate laid face up, including the fragments of royal portraits and currency marks reported in it.
Hand-cut timber — a roof joint from below, a jamb worn smooth at shoulder height, the thickness of a plank door — as evidence of the labour without any person in frame.
The court room in the grounds: one held wide from the back of the room, no movement, nothing approached or isolated, no instrument of punishment in frame.
A wet afternoon in the same rooms: the courtyards running, the channels working, the whole interior flat grey, and the sound of rain inside a plan with no windows.
The closing frame: a single doorway held at bowed-head height until the far room is no longer visible through it.
suggested_location.access: By road, off the Embilipitiya–Rakwana road at Kolonna, about 30 km from Embilipitiya on the Panamure road and around 207 km from Colombo; the approach is ordinary metalled road and a vehicle can reach the grounds. The site is a museum administered by the Department of Archaeology. Opening hours are reported as roughly 08:00 to 16:00, with one source giving Tuesday to Sunday, and reports conflict on whether there is an entrance fee; a ticket enquiry number is published. Visitors are taken through the surviving rooms and courtyards, so a guide or museum officer is normally present. Filming permission is a real and separate requirement and is not implied by admission: the department's published procedure is a written application at least a week in advance stating the sites, the dates and the reason, with a copy of the script where a film or drama is involved, and permits are issued only for work that will not damage the monument. A commercial video fee of the order of Rs 25,000 per site per week is published for cultural-heritage sites, though it is not confirmed that this schedule applies here. Against all of that, a visitor account from April 2025 reports that photography and videography are prohibited at this site outright, including recording the guide's narration. Permission may therefore be refused or granted only on conditions, and nothing in this record has been verified with the department. Aerial work is not appropriate here — a forty-three-room single-storey building does not read from the sky and the film takes no aerial reveal — and if any drone frame were wanted at all it would need its own departmental and civil aviation clearance; the fallback is a ground-level frame through the boundary gateway.
suggested_location.best_time: Mid-morning to early afternoon, when the sun is high enough to fall into small courtyards and reach the floors of the rooms opening off them; the nested-doorway frames want the hour either side of noon. A wet afternoon in either monsoon gives the second look, with no shafts and one flat grey throughout. The closing frame needs late afternoon, as the light leaves the floor. Dry-season months are easier for the approach road; the rain material is worth returning for.

historical_thread.story:
The building stands at Kolonna in the Ratnapura District and is recorded as beginning about 1700, in the reign of Vimaladharmasuriya II (1687–1707), when a building is said to have been erected on the site by Maduwanwela Maha Mohottala. It was not finished then and was never really finished at all. Under Sri Vira Parakrama Narendrasinghe (1707–1739) a Mudaliyar of the family, Maduwanwela Wijesundara Ekanayaka, is recorded as having roofed it with Sinhala clay tiles, and a further rebuilding in permanent stone is dated to about 1725. The house was the seat of six generations of the same family, and each generation added to it. At its largest, in the period given in the sources as 1877 to 1905, it held 121 rooms and 21 inner courtyards — meda midula, open squares punched through a single roofed plan — together with quarters for guards, and stood at the centre of a service estate whose figures are given as two royal grants totalling about 33,184 hectares or 82,000 acres: the Panamure grant of some 21,853 hectares (54,000 acres) attributed to Rajasinghe II and the Maduwanwela grant of some 9,712 hectares (24,000 acres) attributed to Sri Vikrama Rajasinha. Forty-three rooms and seven inner courtyards are what remain.

The layout as it now stands is largely owed to the last prominent figure of the house, Wickramasinghe Wijesundara Ekanayake Abeykoon Mudiyanse Ralahamilage Sir James William Maduwanwela Maha Disawe, born in September 1844 and died on 6 September 1930 of heart disease, who took the Maduwanwela name on inheriting the estate. He rose through colonial service from clerk to Rate Mahatmaya and Korale Mahaththaya and then to Disawe, was knighted, and his wealth is attributed in the sources to timber, gem mining and elephant kraals as well as to the estate. The final expansion of the house is dated to 1905, when the floors were laid as a mosaic of deliberately chipped imported tile and plate from the Netherlands and Britain — fragments carrying royal portraits and currency marks are reported as set into the floor face up. Staircases, door frames and joinery are described as tamarind, jak and satinwood; the walls are clay and brick, lime-plastered, on a black stone platform about three feet above the ground, with the roof in clay tile. The plan has no grand hall: it is a string of small rooms on corridors around the courtyards, and the surviving named rooms recorded in the Sinhala accounts include a drawing room, a long room, a dining room, a smaller and a larger chief's room, the Disawe's bedroom, a storehouse, and a room set aside for women's monthly seclusion. Rainwater is managed by channels cut across the courtyard floors. In the grounds there are further structures: a larger bungalow, an assembly hall, a shrine, ramparts, and the courthouse.

The doorways are the documented peculiarity. Every door in the house is given as about five feet high — one source puts the ceilings themselves at around five feet — and the archways into the grounds are unusually low as well. The explanations in the record do not agree. One is practical and about horses: the gateways were cut low so that a visitor arriving on horseback had to dismount before entering. One is about posture in general: anyone coming in, and particularly a taller foreign official, would be obliged to bend the head and would therefore appear to bow. And one is specific and personal: the last master stood four feet eight inches, so that he alone could ride straight through the stone entrance without lowering his head while Europeans had to bow theirs. A fourth strand in the sources reads the whole arrangement as deliberate anti-colonial defiance, and the epithet 'the dark prince' or 'black prince' attaches to the last master in popular accounts.

The private jurisdiction is also on the record. A courthouse stands in the grounds with bench seating given as a hundred people, where the Disawe sat as both judge and jury on matters of land, livestock and marriage; its original furniture is reported as still in place, and so is the equipment that was used for punishment. A small holding cell is described off the side of it, and the rear wall is reported to carry a faded motto of the British colonial administration. One Sinhala account places the hearing of cases under a large nuga tree in front of the house rather than only inside the court building, and describes imprisonment and corporal punishment among the penalties imposed.

The end of the house as a house is a matter of land law. In 1974 the property and its estate were taken by the Land Reform Commission and placed under the Department of Archaeology, which converted it into a museum; the protected-monument gazette notification for the Kolonna Divisional Secretary's Division is dated 20 September 1974. Sinhala sources give the state takeover as 1964 and the transfer to the Department of Archaeology as 1972, so the dates in the record do not agree. The building is in poor condition: accounts from 2025 describe visible deterioration, damp, failing plaster and a strong smell of bats in the upper structure, and estimates of how much of the original fabric has gone run to about two-thirds. In 2023 some 35 hectares of the surrounding land were reported as leased by the government to the Ceylon Tobacco Company for forest farming.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C005 is not a list of prohibitions. It is a list of the occasions on which greed-rooted minds come up, and the Margaya's enumeration reaches, after food and clothes and music and money, the preparing of the objects one likes — clothes, houses, carriages — and the consuming of them. This house is that clause carried out for two hundred years by six sets of hands. Nothing about it was built at once. It was added to, room onto room, courtyard opened inside courtyard, until a single roofed plan held 121 rooms and 21 open squares, and the additions stop only in 1905 because that is when the last person who was adding stopped. A film of a market has to argue that the reaching it photographs is the reaching the book describes. Here the reaching is the building, and the building is still standing in 1905's final shape.

But the reason this location is right rather than merely apt is the doorway, because the doorway is where the concept becomes a number. The same source that lists the occasions draws its real line by aim, and it draws it, of all places, on appearance: preparing and wearing clothes out of a wish to be beautiful, to win others over, or to appear as a superior person is counted greed-rooted, while wearing something good in order to escape the contempt of onlookers is not counted unwholesome at all. That is an extremely fine line and it runs exactly through this house. Every door is about five feet. Whichever of the recorded explanations is true, the effect is the same: everybody who came in went in bent. What was being obtained was not a good, a taste or a sum of money. It was the shape other people's bodies made on the threshold, and it was specified to the inch and paid for in timber and stone. No other film in this group has a wanting that can be measured with a tape.

And then the record refuses to hand the film its verdict, which is the best thing about it. The three explanations for the door heights are incompatible. If the gateways were cut low so that riders had to dismount, that is security and protocol. If they were cut so that anyone entering would bow, that is deference. If they were cut to four feet eight inches because that is how tall the last master was, then he is the only person in the world the house was comfortable for, and everybody else's bending is a by-product of his convenience — or the point of it, and the record does not say. The sources themselves insist on this limit in a way no amount of footage can get past: the eight greed-rooted minds are separated from each other by the feeling in them, by whether a wrong view is joined to them, and by whether the mind was prompted or arose on its own. Not one of those three is a property of a building. So the film can state the height, state the three reasons, and stop — and the stopping is the teaching, because this group's standing problem is that a camera cannot show greed and here is the most photogenic possible temptation to pretend otherwise.

C021 is what keeps the film honest rather than accusing. Both sources define desire-to-act as the wish to take up or to do, insist that it lacks the stickiness that belongs to greed, and say it takes the side of the mind it joins: it strengthens greed inside a greed-rooted mind and works against greed inside a wholesome one, and developed it becomes a base of success. Effort is defined as mental and not bodily, as the not-turning-back that continues until a started thing is done, and it is explicitly denied the status of a virtue — a boat on a downstream current, carrying a tilted mind along, with doing good compared to carrying a load uphill. Every one of those factors is in this house in quantity. Six generations of deciding, examining, persisting and adding; hand-cut joints in the roof; a floor laid out of smashed imported plate because somebody wanted that floor and saw it through. The identical factors built every school, tank and well in the country. The wood cannot tell you which it was serving, and the sources say plainly that it cannot, which is why this pairing produces a film rather than a judgement.

The subtraction closes it. A hundred and twenty-one rooms became forty-three, and seven courtyards are left of twenty-one, and about two-thirds of the fabric is reported gone. The obvious film there is a decline-and-fall, and that film is forbidden: C061 states that legacy and remembrance are not the teaching, and these sources classify a mind for as long as it lasts and not a person, a family or a line. So the numbers are left as numbers. What the film ends on is the one thing still doing its work — a five-foot doorway in a wall that is standing, which will bend the head of the next person who walks through it, two hundred years after the wanting that cut it to that height stopped being anywhere the camera can look.
what_is_certain: The building is at Kolonna in the Ratnapura District, Sabaragamuwa Province, on the road between Embilipitiya and Rakwana, and is given at coordinates 06°23′21.0″N 80°42′12.5″E.

The site's history is dated to the reign of Vimaladharmasuriya II (1687–1707), with a building said to have been erected there by Maduwanwela Maha Mohottala about 1700; a roofing in Sinhala clay tiles under Sri Vira Parakrama Narendrasinghe (1707–1739) by Mudaliyar Maduwanwela Wijesundara Ekanayaka and a rebuilding in permanent stone about 1725 are recorded.
The house was the seat of six generations of the Maduwanwela family and was expanded repeatedly, the final expansion being dated to 1905.

At its largest, in the period given as 1877–1905, it held 121 rooms and 21 inner courtyards (meda midula), and 43 rooms and 7 courtyards are stated to remain by the English and Sinhala Wikipedia articles.

The doorways are recorded as about five feet high, well under two metres; the archways into the grounds are also unusually low. Multiple independent sources state that the doorways of every one of the 121 rooms stood at less than five feet.

The last prominent figure of the house was Wickramasinghe Wijesundara Ekanayake Abeykoon Mudiyanse Ralahamilage Sir James William Maduwanwela Maha Disawe, born September 1844, died 6 September 1930 of heart disease, who took the Maduwanwela name on inheriting the estate and held the offices of Rate Mahatmaya, Korale Mahaththaya and Disawe.
His height is given in more than one source as four feet eight inches.

The estate is given as royal grants totalling about 33,184 hectares (82,000 acres): a Panamure grant of about 21,853 hectares (54,000 acres) attributed to Rajasinghe II and a Maduwanwela grant of about 9,712 hectares (24,000 acres) attributed to Sri Vikrama Rajasinha. One account gives the holding as an 83,000-acre nindagama inherited from his father.

The floors were laid in 1905 as a mosaic of chipped imported tile and plate, described as coming from the Netherlands, and are reported to include fragments bearing royal portraits and currency marks. Staircases, doorways and joinery are described as tamarind, jak and satinwood; the walls are clay and brick, lime-plastered, on a black stone platform about three feet high, with a clay-tiled roof.

A courthouse stands in the grounds with seating for a hundred people, where the Disawe heard matters of land, livestock and marriage as both judge and jury. Its original furniture and the equipment used for punishments are recorded as still present, and a small holding cell and a faded British colonial-era motto on the rear wall are described.

Named surviving spaces recorded in the Sinhala accounts include a drawing room, a long room, a dining room, a smaller and a larger chief's room, the Disawe's bedroom, a storehouse and a room for women's monthly seclusion; the outbuildings include a larger bungalow, an assembly hall, a shrine and ramparts. Rainwater is carried off by channels cut across the courtyard floors, and the courtyards are the interior's only source of daylight.

In 1974 the house and its estate were taken by the Land Reform Commission and placed under the Department of Archaeology as a museum, and the protected-monument gazette notification for the Kolonna Divisional Secretary's Division is dated 20 September 1974.

The building's present condition is poor. Accounts from 2025 describe visible deterioration, damp, failing plaster and paintings, and a strong smell of bats in the upper structure; one estimate puts the loss of original fabric at about two-thirds. Visitors are shown the surviving rooms and courtyards with antique furniture and household objects on display.
In 2023 about 35 hectares of the surrounding land were reported as leased by the government to the Ceylon Tobacco Company for forest farming.
what_is_disputed: Why the doorways are low. Three explanations are on the record and they are not all compatible, and the film keeps them apart and chooses none. (a) The archways were cut low so that a visitor arriving on horseback had to dismount before entering. (b) Anyone entering, and particularly a taller foreign official, was obliged to bend the head and so appeared to bow. (c) The last master stood four feet eight inches, so that he alone could ride straight through the stone entrance without lowering his head while Europeans had to bow theirs. Explanation (a) is about horses and protocol, (b) is about deference in general, and (c) makes the height a personal fit whose effect on everybody else may have been the purpose or merely the consequence. No source located reconciles them, and none gives a contemporary statement of intent by anyone who built or altered the doors.

How many rooms remain. English Wikipedia and Sinhala Wikipedia give 43; one travel account gives 47; the Sri Lankan Ministry of Education page and a Roar Media article give 42; AmazingLanka and the divaina feature give 40. Courtyards remaining are given as 7 by several sources. 43 is used here as the most widely repeated figure and the discrepancy is not resolved; the correct number should be established on site.

When the state took the property. English sources give 1974, under the Land Reform Commission, with the gazette notification of 20 September 1974. The Sinhala Wikipedia article gives the transfer to the Crown as 1964 and the Department of Archaeology's assumption of responsibility as 1972, and a Sinhala newspaper feature gives 1964. These are not reconciled here.
Where the last master was educated. One account gives St Thomas' College, Colombo; both English Wikipedia articles give Royal College, Colombo. No primary record was consulted.

The height of the ceilings. One Sinhala account states that ceilings throughout were built at about five feet to suit the master's measurements, which is a strong claim and is repeated in secondary writing only. Whether it is the doorways alone or the ceilings as well that are at that height should be measured on site.

The anti-colonial reading of the building. That the low doors and the imported plate set face up in the floor were acts of deliberate defiance against British authority is asserted widely in popular and travel writing, and the epithet 'the dark prince' or 'black prince' attaches to the last master in the same writing. No contemporary source for either was located. The film records that the reading exists and does not adopt it as the meaning of the building, and neither judges nor admires the aristocratic and colonial arrangement the house belonged to.

Whether the courthouse and its contents are open to visitors, and what is actually on display in it. The presence of the furniture and of the punishment equipment is stated in several secondary sources; what a visitor can currently enter, see or be shown was not established. The film's single court-room beat is contingent on this and is cut rather than negotiated if it cannot be filmed as specified.

Whether photography and videography are permitted at all. The Department of Archaeology publishes a written-application procedure for filming at archaeological sites, but a visitor account from April 2025 states that photography and videography are prohibited at this site, including recording the guide's narration. Nothing has been confirmed with the department, and the two positions are left standing as they are.

The estate acreage. Figures of 82,000 acres, 83,000 acres and 80,000 acres (32,000 hectares) all appear, attributed variously to two royal grants or to a single inherited nindagama. The discrepancy is recorded and no figure is treated as established.

Attributions of the various building phases to named individuals and reigns rest on secondary summaries in English and Sinhala, not on inscriptions or archival documents seen in this research. The sequence 'about 1700, about 1725, 1877–1905' is what the secondary record says, and it may compress a good deal.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search on 25 September 2026 and none of it has been checked on the ground, with the Department of Archaeology, or against printed editions, archival documents or inscriptions. The coordinates are the English Wikipedia figures (06°23′21.0″N 80°42′12.5″E) converted to decimal. The construction sequence, the six generations, the room and courtyard counts, the estate grants, the 1905 expansion and floor, the timber species, the named rooms, the courthouse, the 1974 Land Reform Commission takeover and the gazette date of 20 September 1974 all come from the secondary sources listed and were cross-read between at least two of them wherever possible; where they disagree the disagreement is recorded in what_is_disputed and is not resolved. Four separate figures for the rooms remaining (40, 42, 43, 47) and three for the state takeover (1964, 1972, 1974) were found and are all recorded. The five-foot doorway height and the four-feet-eight-inch height of the last master are repeated across several English and Sinhala sources but no measured survey or primary record was located for either, which is why the film measures them itself and says so. The three explanations for the low doorways are reported separately by different sources and no source reconciles them; keeping them apart is deliberate. The 'dark prince' epithet and the anti-colonial reading are recorded as popular attributions and are not used as the meaning of the building. The presence of the punishment equipment is stated in several secondary sources and on the English Wikipedia article and is recorded here for that reason alone; whether any of it is visible to a visitor, and whether it could be filmed under the discipline this film sets itself, is unverified, and the beat is cut rather than softened if not. Access, opening hours and fees are from tourism and travel pages and conflict with each other; the filming procedure is from the Department of Archaeology's own general-services page and the commercial fee figure is from the Central Cultural Fund's filming page, which may not govern this site. The April 2025 report that photography and videography are prohibited here outright is one visitor's published account and is recorded as such, but it is the single most important thing in this block and must be settled with the department before anything else. The last master's full name includes the place name, so the sequence names him only by his knighted forename and the full name is kept inside this block. Five Wikimedia Commons files were confirmed to exist through action=query&titles= before their URLs were written; four of them are 2012 panoramio uploads of the interior, the courtyard, a low gateway and the mosaic floor, and the fifth is an exterior side view. No image of the courthouse or of anything in it was sought or is included. This location puts a second film in the same district as IDEA-0020 within this group, which is flagged rather than resolved; the location was assigned.

unknowns: Filming permission has not been sought and nothing has been confirmed with the Department of Archaeology. One published visitor account from April 2025 states that photography and videography are prohibited at this site outright, including recording the guide's narration, while the department's own published procedure is a written application in advance. Until this is settled the film does not exist, and it is the first thing to check.

The actual door and ceiling heights, and the number of rooms and courtyards now standing, have not been measured or counted. Published figures disagree (40, 42, 43 and 47 rooms; doorways 'about five feet' or 'less than two metres'; ceilings possibly at the same height as the doors).

Whether the courthouse can be entered and filmed, what is in it, and whether the punishment equipment is on open display, is unknown. The film's one beat there is contingent and is cut rather than negotiated.
Interior light levels and whether any supplementary lighting is permitted are unverified, and the whole treatment depends on what the courtyards give.
The building's structural condition, the bat population and whether parts of the plan are closed to visitors are known only from 2025 press and visitor accounts.
The date the state took the property (1964, 1972 or 1974) and the last master's schooling are unresolved between sources, and no primary record was consulted for any of the building's phases.
Whether the surrounding land leased in 2023 affects the setting or the approach is unknown.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Claude's suggestion and awaits Chathura's verdict; its supporting detail, including the historical thread, is desk research by web search and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
